title: Hospital stays, tests and medical procedures
lede: A hospital stay adds changing staff, fasting, pain, alarms and loss of control over routine. Preparing communication and consent reduces risk, not only distress.

p: Ask for written information: where to go, how long it takes, fasting requirements, clothing, whether a companion can attend, sedation and what will happen afterwards. Prepare a communication sheet and ask which objects or supports can be brought in.

Ley 41/2002 requires free and voluntary consent after information has been provided; disabled people must be offered support and accessible formats so that the person themselves can participate and give consent.

Keep AAC available, explain before touching, reduce changes of professional where possible, group procedures together if clinically feasible, and record which signs indicate pain or deterioration for that particular person.

title: Anxiety, panic and mental health crises: what to do and where to seek help
lede: An intense crisis first requires safety and reduced demands. Not all anxiety is an emergency, and not every emergency can be resolved with breathing techniques.

p: Reduce questions, offer a safer or less stimulating place, use short sentences and avoid arguing about whether there is ‘a reason’ to be afraid. If the person knows a strategy that helps them, make it available; do not impose physical contact.

Record triggers, duration, physical symptoms and what helped. If it recurs, restricts everyday life or changes in nature, seek professional assessment to distinguish anxiety, panic, medication effects, physical problems or other conditions.
In Spain, 024 is free, confidential and available 24/7 for people experiencing suicidal thoughts or behaviour and for those close to them. In an immediate life-threatening emergency, call 112.

title: Pain, gastrointestinal health and body signals
lede: Abdominal pain, constipation, reflux, headache or musculoskeletal pain should be assessed and treated even when a person communicates discomfort in an unusual way.

sections.h: Do not assume it is behaviour
p: A change in sleep, irritability, food refusal, repetitive movement or reduced skills may accompany pain. If the person finds it difficult to identify or express sensations, ask using specific options and look for changes from their usual pattern.

Record the time, location, intensity using a scale the person understands, food, bowel movements, menstruation, medication, activity and what makes it better or worse. Take the record to the professional.

Sudden severe pain, dehydration, bleeding, breathing difficulty, a major change in consciousness or other warning signs require urgent medical attention. Neurodivergence should not be used to explain away a physical symptom without investigating it.

title: Epilepsy and other recurring episodes: what to prepare
lede: When a person has epilepsy or another condition involving recurring episodes, the people who live or work with them need a simple, up-to-date plan.

p: Record how episodes usually begin, their usual duration, rescue medication if prescribed, when to give it, when to call 112, contacts and what to do afterwards. It should reflect instructions from the healthcare team, not generic advice from the internet.

sections.h: At school, work or leisure activities
p: Agree who stores the medication, who knows how to administer it, how privacy will be protected and how temporary or new staff will be informed. Do not exclude activities by default: assess the risk of each specific activity.

Record its duration and characteristics. If it is the first episode, lasts longer than stated in the plan, repeats without recovery, or involves injury or breathing difficulty, seek urgent care in line with healthcare instructions.

title: Menstruation, menopause and sexual health
lede: Hormonal changes can affect pain, sleep, temperature, energy, mood and sensory tolerance. Not every change should be attributed to neurodivergence.

p: Keep menstrual products in several places, try different textures and formats, use reminders if anticipating the change is difficult, and record pain or bleeding. If menstrual hygiene is difficult, practise the sequence outside an urgent situation.

Record changes in the menstrual cycle, hot flushes, sleep, mood and functioning. Take specific information to primary care or gynaecology. Symptoms may need assessment and individualised treatment options.
Information and consent must be understandable and respect privacy and autonomy. Gender identity should not be used to deny care related to organs or bodily functions that the person has.

title: ARFID, eating disorders and pica: when everyday support needs clinical care
lede: Selective eating, ARFID, anorexia, bulimia, binge-eating disorder, OSFED and pica are not the same. Sharing a difficulty with food does not mean the same treatment should be assumed.

p: Weight loss or altered growth, fainting, signs of dehydration or nutritional deficiency, dependence on supplements or enteral nutrition, binge eating, vomiting or compensatory behaviours, intense fear related to weight or body shape, or repeated consumption of non-food substances.

sections.h: What to take to the appointment
p: An accurate record of food and drinks, supplements, gastrointestinal symptoms, growth information if available, the reason for food refusal and differences between home and other settings. Do not ‘improve’ the record to make the diet look more varied.
Nutritional safety comes first. Avoid turning every meal into an improvised exposure exercise or a power struggle. The specific approach depends on the diagnosis and medical status.

title: Communication without speech, mutism, apraxia, stammering and difficult speech
lede: Not speaking, speaking very little, stammering or being unable to speak in a particular situation are different experiences. The common rule is not to confuse access to speech with understanding or the ability to make decisions.

p: Allow time, ask one question at a time, allow writing or pointing, do not automatically finish the sentences of someone who stammers, and do not require spoken language as proof that something has been understood.

Agree an alternative way to respond before a situation of speech loss or blockage occurs: tablet, keyboard, cards, gestures, communication board or a support person. AAC should remain available even if the person speaks at other times.
Reduce pressure and allow non-spoken responses. Rewarding, punishing or making the person the centre of attention so that they ‘finally speak’ increases demands and can make anxiety worse.

title: Sensory overload, hyperacusis, misophonia and auditory processing
lede: Noise, light, smell, touch and movement can be difficult for different reasons. Hyperacusis, misophonia, auditory processing disorder (APD) and sensory overload are not synonyms, although some everyday adjustments may overlap.

p: Use headphones or hearing protection when safe, take breaks away from the environment, sit away from speakers, provide advance information about alarms or lights, shop at quieter times and allow unnecessary stimuli to be switched off.

sections.h: Do not use hearing protection all day by default
p: Constant hearing protection may not be appropriate for everyone and can make communication or safety more difficult. For hyperacusis, APD or new symptoms, audiology or ENT assessment may be appropriate depending on the situation.

Describe the stimulus and the solution: ‘I need a seat away from the speaker’ is more useful than ‘I have sensory sensitivity’. In services open to the public, reasonable measures may form part of accessibility.
